A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICQL research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, moved, added, and removed content.

before.justification: v1 reports original ICQL experiments on MuJoCo, Adroit, and Kitchen tasks, including retrieval and architecture-depth ablations and appendix analyses of learned critics.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds architecture comparisons, computational measurements, retrieval diagnostics, and expanded Q-value analyses.

M1.justification: v1 Appendix E proposes a return-to-go-augmented SARSA update and modified prompt for sparse rewards. v2 removes this extension and retains the reward-only construction, narrowing the proposed method's scope. The central retrieval mechanism, linear Transformer, IQL objectives, and TD3+BC variant remain; moving their equations into Section 3.3 is not a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 18 MuJoCo, Adroit, and Kitchen datasets. The additional comparisons and diagnostics use these retained datasets without introducing a new task, population, domain, or input scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix H.1 and Table 7 add evaluated comparisons with RA-DT, ReBRAC, DMG, FQL, and QC to the original BC, DT, TD3+BC, CQL, and IQL baselines. Section 4.3.4 also compares the proposed linear Transformer with linear-MLP and standard-Transformer alternatives.

E3.justification: v2 introduces computational evaluation protocols measuring training and inference latency, GFLOPs, peak memory, and cached versus uncached retrieval. Its scaling study crosses context lengths 10–40 with layer counts 10, 20, 30, and 40. These are additional protocols; the original million-step training budget, batch size 256, ten evaluation episodes, and performance-ablation grids remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds module-architecture ablations, computational scaling analyses, Hammer failure diagnostics, retrieval-distance distributions across context lengths, and expanded comparisons with SAC Q-values. It removes v1's learned-parameter distribution analysis and Figure 7. The intermediate-layer output analysis is retained in Appendix H.7, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-seed reporting and standard deviations for the main ICQL scores, with five-seed averages for the TD3+BC variant. No increased run count, confidence interval, or significance-testing procedure is introduced. The new Table 7 repeats the five-seed mean-and-standard-deviation caption but displays only point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline, architecture, computational, and diagnostic results. Existing reported values also change: Table 1 revises Hopper-Medium-Expert ICQL from 108.8±4.5 to 111.0±0.6, and Table 2 revises Door-Human state-similar retrieval from 12.89 to 17.1, changing its ranking against reward-filtered retrieval. Default-setting ablation scores are also revised; the PDFs do not establish why these values changed.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the neighborhood radius from the minimum retrieved distance to the maximum, and Appendix H.5 adds a formal connection between retrieval size and radius. The return-to-go update derivation is removed. The principal local-error bounds, policy-gap theorem, and their proofs otherwise remain substantially unchanged; Appendix C still retains minimum-distance expressions.

C1.justification: The advertised MuJoCo improvement changes from 8.6% to 8.8%. The introduction also softens the assertion that every control task inherently decomposes into subtasks to a statement about many tasks. The central contributions concerning contextual Q-learning, unsupervised local modeling, and near-optimal greedy-policy extraction remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops explanations of Hammer failures through coverage and reward quality, computational tradeoffs, and how retrieval size affects locality. Its conclusion explicitly identifies retrieval quality in high-dimensional spaces as a limitation and proposes learned retrievers. It removes the earlier Kitchen-quadrant interpretation and the interpretation of parameter distributions as adaptive learning rates.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents precomputing and caching retrieval indices, reports dataset sizes and detailed runtime measurements, and states that added baselines follow official implementations. These are disclosures, not evidence that the retained experiments changed. The existing network specifications, optimizer-related settings, and hyperparameter tables remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of RA-DT, ReBRAC, DMG, FQL, and QC, while Appendix A.2 adds relevant work by Ahn and Dai. This updates the surrounding literature without substantially redefining the original positioning of local contextual value estimation against global models and trajectory-based policy learning. Publication-metadata updates are not new cited works.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, related work, and much appendix prose receive extensive language editing. The prompt and weight-matrix construction moves into the main text, pseudocode moves to the appendix, and implementation details and additional experiments become separate appendix sections. These changes substantially reorganize the explanation of retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adds architecture and extended-baseline tables, multiple computational tables, retrieval-distance displays, and expanded Q-value visualizations. Figure 3 uses normalized color scales and changes its dataset label from Walker2d-Medium-Replay to Walker2d-Medium. The parameter-distribution figure is removed, while the intermediate-output plot is relocated as Figure 10.

improvement.justification: The architecture controls, broader baseline comparisons, computational measurements, and failure analyses make v2 more informative and better qualify its applicability. Clearer organization also helps explain the method. However, new reporting problems temper these gains: Table 7 reports an ICQL overall average of 69.7 although its 18 displayed scores average approximately 63.2, and its promised standard deviations are absent. The evidence supports a net improvement, but these inconsistencies limit its strength.
